there were five observational studies that identified 18 RFs for the occurrence of PUs in people with SCI.
the most important risk factors are: (1) the severity of injury; (2) the level of injury; (3) age; and (4) the presence of comorbidities.
the key risk factors for the prevention of pressure ulcers (PUs) in people with spinal injury (SCI) include: age, sex, marital status, level of injury, duration of injury and level of independence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and management of risk factors for pressure ulcers in adults with spinal injury.
understanding the development and recurrence patterns of pressure ulcers (PUs) for people with spinal cord injury.
the development and validation of a risk assessment tool to assist clinicians in the early identification of patients who are at risk of developing pressure ulcers.

the risk of developing a PU is influenced by a number of factors, which are not yet well understood, and that further research is required to determine the most important factors.
there is a lack of conclusive evidence for the development of a risk assessment tool specific for people with SCI.
the RFs identified in the literature for the general PU and SCI populations are similar, but the RFs for SCI are not well established.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of PU development and recurrence for people with SCI is influenced by a range of factors including neurological, functional and clinical factors.
a number of risk factors are associated with pressure ulcer development and recurrence in people with SCI.
the development and recurrence risk of PUs is multifactorial and complex, with a range of factors that may be important.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk factors are the same for both SCI and non-SCI populations.
the risk of pressure ulcer recurrence is not well understood and there is an urgent need to develop and test a risk assessment tool for people with SCI.
there is no single RF for the development and/or recurrence of PUs in people with SCI, rather there are multiple RFs that interact and influence PU risk.
